# Self-Correction: What It Means and What It Doesn't {#sec-self-correction}

Target ~4,000 words. See `research/00-book-outline.md` Chapter 5. Open with the OpenReview *"Tiny Silent Hallucinations in Agentic AI"* paper — the field's most under-discussed 2026 result.

## What "self-correcting" actually means

- Self-correction decomposes into three concrete subsystems, not one capability:
  - **Detection** — knowing you're wrong.
  - **Repair** — fixing it.
  - **Escalation** — failing safely to HITL when detection or repair can't close the loop.
- Most production failures are **detection failures**, not repair failures. The model never noticed.
- The standard marketing pitch — "the model corrects its own mistakes" — collapses all three into one. The vendors that take production seriously instrument all three separately.

## The reflection loop, mechanically

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Reflection loop with confidence gating"
flowchart TD
    A[Extraction] --> B[Self-critique]
    B --> C{Confidence above threshold?}
    C -- Yes --> D[Output]
    C -- No --> E{Retries left?}
    E -- Yes --> F[Re-prompt with critique]
    F --> A
    E -- No --> G[Escalate to HITL]
```

- The retry budget is a real engineering parameter, not magic. Typical values: 2–4 retries before escalation.
- The confidence threshold is calibrated, not chosen. Calibration data needs to match production distribution.
- A reflection loop **with no external oracle** is a model becoming more confident in its first answer.

## Confidence gating: real vs. theatre

- Confidence scores from VLMs are not calibrated probabilities. They are an ordinal signal at best.
- The classic failure mode: high-confidence wrong answers. Model is wrong, model is confident, threshold-based gating passes the answer through.
- What real confidence gating needs: an **external oracle** — schema validator, layout cross-check, KB lookup, or a different model's opinion.
- The Databricks "$10,000 → $3,000" hallucination is a textbook high-confidence-wrong failure. The loop didn't catch it because the loop didn't know the right answer.

## A failure taxonomy

A 3×N matrix of failure modes, grouped by which subsystem broke.

- **Detection failures:**
  - Silent hallucination — model is wrong, model doesn't notice.
  - Confidence-score miscalibration — model is unsure but reports high confidence.
  - Out-of-distribution blindness — document is unlike training data, model doesn't realize it.
- **Repair failures:**
  - Repair-thrash — every retry produces a different wrong answer.
  - Reflection drift — the critique itself drifts further from truth across iterations.
- **Escalation failures:**
  - No HITL path — the model escalates to a queue that nobody monitors.
  - Wrong-stakes escalation — the system escalates everything (HITL overload) or nothing (silent acceptance).

(See research notes section 10 for production-incident retrospective sources.)

## What self-correction does not do

- Does not fix **bad source documents**. Garbage in is still garbage out, just with more API calls.
- Does not detect **missing semantic context**. An invoice that's missing a field is correctly extracted as "this field is missing." Whether the field *should* exist is a different judgment.
- Does not provide a **safety net** for high-stakes decisions. HITL still belongs there. The reflection loop reduces HITL volume, it does not replace HITL.

## Named takes

> *"Self-correction is not 'the model will figure it out.' It is three concrete subsystems — detection, repair, escalation. If your vendor talks about it as one thing, they have one of the three working."*

> *"A reflection loop with no out-of-loop ground truth is a model becoming more confident in its first answer. Call it what it is."*
